tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (Lupori et al., 'Towards a High-Performance RISC-V Emulator', 2018, IEEE Xplore 8748908) reports the SBT at 1.12x slowdown versus RV8 3.16x and QEMU 7.07x (figure caption seen only as a search snippet), and the repo carries the harness (mibench/genmake.py, scripts/auto/measure.py, scripts/auto/config.py) plus committed result CSVs that show the same ordering; no CPU model is stated anywhere reachable, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Committed result CSVs (mibench/results): geomean slowdown versus native 32-bit x86 of 1.08x (abi mapping) and 1.23x (locals mapping) over 19 MiBench programs, counting only cycles spent in the benchmark's own code (x86-avx-gcchf.csv 'x' columns, derived from page data); with libc time included the SBT geomeans are 1.02x abi and 1.11x locals (x86-avx-gcchf-wlibc.csv, derived from page data). QEMU 6.13x total-time geomean over 19 programs (qemu_slowdown.csv geomean row) and rv8 2.85x over the 10 programs it could run (rv8_slowdown.csv geomean row; the other 9 rows are zero-filled placeholders). On the same 10 programs: SBT abi 1.10x, SBT locals 1.24x, QEMU 5.39x, rv8 2.85x (derived from page data). Per-benchmark example: rijndael-encode 14.54x under QEMU, 4.51x under rv8, 1.11x for the SBT (abi). The 2018 paper gives an SBT average of 1.12x versus 3.16x for RV8 (commit 1d4d1ee) and 7.07x for QEMU (v2.12.0-835-g360a7809d2-dirty) (search snippet of the ResearchGate figure caption only; paper not opened).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -fno-exceptions for both RISC-V and native binaries (scripts/auto/config.py: GOPTS.cc and rvcc = gcc, _O = -O3); RISC-V binaries use -march=rv32g with the ilp32d hard-float ABI; native x86 binaries are 32-bit (i686-linux-gnu-gcc-7 when present, otherwise gcc -m32) with -mfpmath=sse -mavx; the SBT lowers translated code with LLVM llc -relocation-model=static -march=x86 -mattr=avx; static linking is forced only for rv8 and OVP runs (GOPTS.static), QEMU runs as qemu-riscv32 -L <sysroot>. gcc, LLVM, QEMU and rv8 versions are not stated in the repo (the paper snippet names RV8 commit 1d4d1ee and QEMU v2.12.0-835-g360a7809d2-dirty).
corrections.workload: MiBench programs (dijkstra, crc32, rijndael encode/decode, sha, adpcm encode/decode, stringsearch, blowfish encode/decode, basicmath, bitcount, fft std/inv, patricia, susan smoothing/edges/corners, lame; 19 rows) built for RV32 and translated ahead of time to 32-bit x86 (AVX) with LLVM, run time measured with perf as slowdown versus the same program built natively for 32-bit x86; QEMU and rv8 run the RV32 binaries.
corrections.caveats: CPU model is not stated in anything reachable (the paper is blocked in this environment), so tier A is unmet; the paper numbers (1.12x, 3.16x, 7.07x) come only from a search snippet and differ from the committed CSVs. Metric mismatch in the committed CSVs: scripts/auto/measure.py multiplies run time by the fraction of perf cycles in the benchmark's own DSO for the SBT runs (x86-avx-gcchf.csv, so libc time is excluded), while --rv32 emulator runs disable perf_libc and use total time (qemu.csv and rv8.csv show 100% for every row); the like-for-like total-time file x86-avx-gcchf-wlibc.csv gives 1.02x abi and 1.11x locals, so the win holds either way. The rv8 column covers only 10 of 19 programs (notes/rv8: basicmath crash, bitcount wrong result, fft never ends, patricia does not build, susan and lame fail) and its geomean row is over those 10; QEMU's 6.13x is over all 19 (5.39x on the same 10, derived). rv8 and QEMU are dynamic translators that pay translation cost at run time, while the SBT output is native x86 produced ahead of time, so the comparison is not like for like. github.com/OpenISA/riscv-sbt now redirects to github.com/lmcad-unicamp/riscv-sbt (current owner; same 18 stars and 5 forks). The OpenISA-input SBT results (x86-oi_slowdown.csv) are a separate translator and not this claim. Last commit 2019-03-06.

notes: Committed CSV geomeans re-derived and match the record (abi 1.075, locals 1.233 over 19 programs). Shortcomings to record: no CPU model; paper reached only via snippet; SBT CSV excludes libc time while the QEMU/rv8 CSVs use total time (with-libc SBT file still shows 1.02x/1.11x); rv8 measured on 10 of 19 programs; static versus dynamic translation is not like for like; abandoned since 2019. The repo URL now redirects to lmcad-unicamp/riscv-sbt; consider a repo_url override.

tier_reason: Only numbers are one first-party status-talk slide (doc/slides/ANL_Summer_Status_Update.pdf, slide 11, 23.07.2018): matrix-multiply bar chart with Default about 660 microseconds and best random-search configuration G about 445, captioned 'Up to 1.48x Speedup, aka 32.7% improvement!'; no compiler, flags, CPU, matrix size or committed results, and the baseline is the tool's own untuned configuration.

corrections.caveats: The only numbers are one slide from a July 2018 status talk: a single kernel (matrix multiply), 'Default' baseline not defined on the slide, no compiler, flags, CPU model or matrix size, and the 1.48x is 'up to', i.e. the best of the random-search configurations; the slide does not say whether tuning time and JIT compile cost are included, and its y-axis starts at 400 microseconds, which visually exaggerates the gap. In the current code (include/tuner/RandomTuner.h) the first configuration the random tuner tries is genDefaultConfig, with the codegen optimisation level defaulting to 3 (CodegenOptions.h), so 'Default' is probably the JIT's own untuned pipeline rather than an ahead-of-time clang -O3 build, but the 2018 code behind the slide is not pinned. The README calls the project 'an early-phase experiment in online autotuning' and gives no speedups. The repo has benchmark sources (benchmark/benchmark.cpp with Google Benchmark; CMake builds atjit-benchmark-O0/O1/O2/O3 AOT variants) but no committed results, so a run would be needed to compare against clang -O3 ahead-of-time or Easy::jit. No thesis or paper with numbers was found. Last commit 2019-08-29; CI moved to gitlab.com/kavon1/atJIT.

notes: Slide 11 rendered and read: chart matches the record (Default about 660 us, G about 445 us, 1.48x). Shortcomings to record: baseline is the tool's own untuned config, not a named incumbent; single kernel; best-of-random-search 'up to' figure; no methodology; truncated y-axis; early experiment, abandoned since 2019.
